result.summary: Hesiod opens the Theogony by invoking the Muses of Helicon, who dance, sing and praise the gods. He tells how they appeared to him as a shepherd and gave him a laurel rod and the gift of song, then describes their birth to Zeus and Mnemosyne and the blessings they bring to kings and singers.

scenes.title: The Muses dance on Helicon
scenes.summary: The Muses bathe, dance on Helicon and go out by night singing the praises of the gods.

scenes.title: Hesiod receives the gift of song
scenes.summary: While Hesiod tends lambs, the Muses rebuke shepherds, give him a laurel rod and a divine voice, and bid him sing of the gods.
scenes.stakes: Hesiod is addressed as a lowly shepherd; his calling as poet depends on the goddesses' favour.

scenes.title: The Muses sing on Olympus
scenes.summary: The poet turns to the Muses' song in Olympus, which delights Zeus and tells of gods, men and giants.

scenes.title: Birth of the Muses
scenes.summary: Zeus lies nine nights with Mnemosyne in Pieria, and she bears the nine Muses, who sing to Zeus after his victory over Cronos.

scenes.title: Gifts of the Muses
scenes.summary: The nine Muses are named, and their gifts to just kings and to singers who ease men's sorrows are described.

notable_quotes.reason: The Muses admit they can speak falsehoods that seem true, a famous statement about poetic truth.
Describes song as a relief from sorrow, a classic statement of poetry's power.

analysis.text: The proem grounds poetic authority in divine inspiration: the poet sings truth only because the Muses grant it, and the song begins and ends with the gods.
The passage links kings and poets as gifts of Zeus and the Muses, reflecting an archaic Greek view of just rule, and gives an early account of a poet's calling.

legacy.text: Invoking the Muses at the start of a poem became a standard convention of Greek and Roman epic and later European poetry, as in Milton's Paradise Lost.
The word music derives from the Greek name of the Muses, and museum from their shrines.

fun_facts.text: Hesiod places his own meeting with the Muses on Helicon, making this one of the earliest first-person accounts of a poet's initiation in Western literature.

language_notes.text: Permessus, the Horse's Spring (Hippocrene) and Olmeius are springs and streams near Mount Helicon in Boeotia, sacred to the Muses.
'Mere bellies' means people who think only of eating; the Muses insult the shepherds as greedy and shameful.
'Oak or stone' is a proverbial expression for irrelevant, old-fashioned tales; the poet breaks off his digression and returns to his theme.
Mnemosyne is the Greek word for Memory; the poet glosses it in brackets. Eleuther is a hill region on the Boeotian border.
Refers to Zeus's overthrow of his father Cronos and the Titans, after which he assigned each god a domain and honours.
'Heaven-nourished' means raised by the gods, so kings are portrayed as divinely favoured.

context_notes.text: Hesiod names himself and describes his poetic calling, a rare personal moment in early Greek poetry.
The laurel rod is a staff of authority, like a poet's sceptre; laurel was later associated with Apollo.
The Graces were goddesses of charm and beauty, often attending the Muses and Aphrodite.
The nine Muses later became patrons of particular arts, such as epic (Calliope), history (Cleio) and astronomy (Urania).

literary_notes.text: The poem opens by invoking the Muses, the traditional source of a poet's inspiration and authority.
The Muses admit they can speak falsehoods that seem true, warning that poetry is not automatically reliable and claiming Hesiod's truth.
The goddesses' voice is called 'lily-like', blending sound and image to suggest delicate beauty.
The nine nights anticipate nine Muses, linking the number of the conception to the number of daughters.
Listing the nine Muses by name is a typical epic technique that gives the divine group order and authority.
The sorrowing man is set against the soothed listener, showing how song makes grief fade.
